content: Tinea capitis, also referred to as herpes tonsurans, ringworm of the hair, ringworm of the scalp, scalp ringworm, or tinea tonsurans, is a superficial fungal infection (dermatophytosis) affecting the scalp. This condition is primarily caused by dermatophytes belonging to the Trichophyton and Microsporum genera, which invade the hair shaft. Clinically, tinea capitis often presents as one or more patches of hair loss, sometimes with a characteristic black dot pattern due to broken-off hairs. These patches may be accompanied by inflammation, scaling, pustules, and itching. The condition is uncommon in adults and predominantly affects pre-pubertal children, with boys being more frequently affected than girls. At least eight species of dermatophytes are associated with tinea capitis. Trichophyton infections are more common in regions such as Central America, the United States, and parts of Western Europe, while Microsporum infections are more prevalent in South America, Southern and Central Europe, Africa, and the Middle East. Tinea capitis is contagious and can be transmitted through direct contact with infected humans, animals, or contaminated objects. The fungus can also exist in a carrier state on the scalp without causing clinical symptoms. Treatment requires oral antifungal agents, with griseofulvin being the most commonly used medication. Newer antifungal drugs, such as terbinafine, itraconazole, and fluconazole, are also gaining acceptance. Symptoms of tinea capitis may include thickened, scaly, and sometimes boggy swellings, or expanding raised red rings resembling ringworm. Common symptoms include severe scalp itching, dandruff, and bald patches where the fungus has invaded the skin. The condition can mimic dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis. In the United States, the highest incidence is observed in school-aged boys. There are three types of tinea capitis based on the causative microorganism and symptomatology: microsporiasis, trichophytosis, and favus. In microsporiasis, the lesion begins as a small red papule around a hair shaft, which later becomes scaly. The hair eventually breaks off 1–3 mm above the scalp. Historically, Microsporum audouinii was the primary causative agent, but in Europe, Microsporum canis is now more common. This fungus is often transmitted from sick cats and kittens, though person-to-person contact or sharing contaminated brushes and combs can also spread the infection. In the United States, trichophytosis is usually caused by Trichophyton tonsurans, while Trichophyton violaceum is more common in Eastern Europe, Africa, and India. This type of infection causes dry, non-inflammatory patches that are often angular in shape. When hairs break off at the follicle opening, black dots remain. Favus, caused by Trichophyton schoenleinii, is endemic in South Africa and the Middle East. It is characterized by yellowish, circular, cup-shaped crusts (scutula) grouped in patches resembling a honeycomb, with a hair projecting from the center. These lesions enlarge and become crusted, with the characteristic appearance visible only at the scab's edge. Diagnosing tinea capitis can be challenging, as it may resemble other skin conditions like psoriasis or seborrheic dermatitis. Diagnosis is confirmed through microscopic examination and microbial culture of epilated hairs. A Wood's lamp examination can reveal bright green to yellow-green fluorescence in hairs infected by Microsporum species, while Trichophyton schoenleinii infections may show a dull green or blue-white fluorescence. Trichoscopy of Microsporum canis infections reveals characteristic small comma-shaped hairs. Histopathology of scalp biopsies shows sparse fungal distribution in the stratum corneum and hyphae extending down the hair follicle, often associated with inflammatory tissue reactions. The preferred treatment for tinea capitis is oral griseofulvin, a fungistatic agent derived from the fungus Penicillium griseofulvin. It works by disrupting the fungal microtubular system, interfering with the mitotic spindle and cytoplasmic microtubules. The recommended pediatric dosage is 10 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks, which may be increased to 20 mg/kg/day for infections caused by Trichophyton tonsurans or cases unresponsive to initial treatment. Unlike other fungal skin infections treatable with topical therapies, griseofulvin must be taken orally to penetrate the hair shaft where the fungus resides. The treatment success rate is high, ranging from 88–100%. Other oral antifungal treatments, such as terbinafine, itraconazole, and fluconazole, offer shorter treatment durations but may carry risks of rare side effects like liver toxicity or drug interactions. These newer treatments are also more expensive than griseofulvin. The FDA has approved terbinafine hydrochloride (Lamisil) for use in children aged four years and older. This medication is available as antifungal granules that can be sprinkled on food. However, Lamisil carries a risk of hepatotoxicity and may cause a metallic taste in the mouth. The pathophysiology of tinea capitis involves fungal growth from the site of inoculation into the stratum corneum, where keratin is invaded. Dermatophytes produce keratinase, enabling them to use keratin as a nutrient source. Infected hairs become brittle, and broken hairs are clinically evident after three weeks. There are three types of infection: ectothrix, endothrix, and favus. Ectothrix infections are characterized by fungal spores (arthroconidia) on the hair shaft's exterior, often fluorescing greenish-yellow under a Wood's lamp. Endothrix infections involve arthroconidia restricted to the hair shaft, with the cuticle remaining intact and no fluorescence. Favus causes crusting on the skin surface and hair loss. Epidemiologically, tinea capitis is a contagious disease endemic in many countries, primarily affecting pre-pubertal children aged 6–10 years, with a higher prevalence in males. The disease rarely persists past age sixteen. Spread occurs through direct contact with infected individuals or indirectly via contaminated objects (fomites). In the United States, tinea capitis affects 3–8% of the pediatric population, with up to one-third of households in contact with an infected person harboring the disease asymptomatically. The causative fungal species vary by geographic region and may change over time. For example, Microsporum audouinii was the predominant agent in North America and Europe until the 1950s, but Trichophyton tonsurans is now more common in the United States and increasingly prevalent in Europe and the United Kingdom. This shift is attributed to the widespread use of griseofulvin, which is more effective against Microsporum audouinii than Trichophyton tonsurans, as well as changes in immigration patterns and increased international travel. Trichophyton violaceum has also become more prevalent, particularly in urban populations in the United Kingdom and Europe.
